content: 1. The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Specifications (JMPS) evaluates new impurities, toxicological, and ecotoxicological profiles by comparing them with the original data. Based on this comparison, the JMPS recommends specific actions to the FAO/WHO. 2. If insufficient data or unacceptable material quality is provided, the new submission is rejected. 3. If the submission and material quality are acceptable and no specification changes are needed, the names of the proposers are added to the evaluation and published by FAO/WHO. 4. If the material quality is acceptable but specification changes are required, the listed proposers collaborate to draft a revised specification. If agreement cannot be reached, the JMPS recommends appropriate actions to FAO/WHO. 5. FAO and WHO prioritize their three-year program for specification development and review based on criteria such as locust control, vector-borne disease control, and addressing newly discovered health or environmental hazards. 6. Specifications are reviewed for active ingredients or impurities with serious hazards, rejected re-registration, or changes in manufacturing processes. They are also reviewed for products under international agreements like PIC or POP, or for those withdrawn due to lack of supporting data. 7. Specifications older than 10 years or for pesticides no longer marketed are reviewed. Tentative or interim specifications are also subject to review. 8. Specifications aim to describe quantifiable parameters with clear limits, avoiding subjective judgment by buyers. Non-quantifiable elements are included in notes but not as part of the specification. 9. Technical-grade active ingredients should be as pure as economically feasible to minimize formulation, toxicity, and phytotoxicity issues. Long-term quality improvements are often prioritized despite potential challenges. 10. Formulation specifications consider properties relevant to efficacy, operator safety, and environmental impact. Standard tests may not exist for all parameters, necessitating the development of new methods. 11. Proposals for specification limits stricter than guidelines are usually acceptable, while less stringent limits require justification and supporting data. 12. Specifications for co-formulated products must address the purity and impurity content of each active ingredient. Analytical methods may need modification for such products. 13. Sampling for compliance testing must represent the entire pesticide lot. Recommendations for sampling are provided in the guidelines. 14. The title and description of a pesticide specification must clearly identify the technical or formulated product, using ISO or IUPAC chemical names where applicable. 15. Identity tests for active ingredients must include at least two methods to ensure clear identification, especially for salts or mixtures of isomers. Analytical methods must be peer-validated. 16. Active ingredient content is expressed in g/kg or g/L at 20 ± 2°C, with tolerances accounting for manufacturing, sampling, and analytical variations. Positive deviations may be allowed if justified by storage degradation compensation. 17. Specifications for co-formulated products may include clauses for isomer ratios if not defined by ISO names. Analytical methods for isomer determination must also be peer-validated. 18. The JMPS considers regulatory practices in countries where the active ingredient is registered when evaluating manufacturer proposals for specifications.
